#### Logging In

When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the command prints. The login URL the command prints opens in the host's browser, once, and nothing else ever opens one.
Only the login command's own output is read for it, from when the command starts, never what the image build prints before it, nor anything Podman prints while it pulls, builds, or starts the container, all of which is shown as text and never opened, its URLs at most clickable links. And only a URL that is the harness's login is opened: the first one the login command prints that leads to its sign-in, as Claude Code's to claude.ai or console.anthropic.com, Codex's to auth.openai.com, or OpenCode's to the provider it is logging in with, or a localhost callback it asks to be visited. Any other URL it prints, as a link to documentation, release notes, or a package's homepage, is only shown. A login opens at most one URL by itself, the first such one; any later is shown as a link, for the user to click. Where no URL is recognized, nothing opens, and the view shows every URL the command printed as a link instead.
Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is cancelled or fails.
A login needs the image, as any run in a container does, and the first login on a machine is most often the first thing to need it. So the login view builds it first where it isn't there or is out of date, showing "Preparing environment" and what the build prints as it goes, and starts the login command only once the build has succeeded. A build that fails shows why in the login view, as a failed build says it, with a "Try again" button that builds it again, and starts no login.
The harness's volume is ready for it before its first login: created by the application with `podman volume create` where it isn't there, and mounted so that the user the container runs as owns it and can write it, as with Podman's `:U` option, never left owned by root where the harness runs as the user. The container's HOME, where the volume is mounted beneath it, as ~/.claude, is a directory that user owns, as is the volume, so the login command can write its credentials there on the first login as on any other.
Which harness is logged in is always the one the run needs: the harness of the run's project, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, never Claude Code by default, and never another project's. A run, a Welcome check, or a login asked for checks that harness's own volume alone, by its own credentials file: Claude Code's `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, Codex's `~/.codex/auth.json`, and OpenCode's `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`, each counting as logged in only where the file is there and not empty. Its login view is titled for it, "Log in to Codex" and the like, and runs its own login command, `claude /login` for Claude Code, `codex login` for Codex, and `opencode auth login` for OpenCode, in a container with that harness's volume mounted, so its credentials land where its runs read them. A run never asks for one harness's login while it is about to run another.
A run that fails because its harness isn't logged in says so, naming the harness, "Codex isn't logged in", with a "Log in" button that shows its login view, rather than the harness's raw error alone. A login that fails says why in the command's own words, its exit status, and which harness it was for, and the run waiting on it fails saying the same. The login view, the Welcome check, and the Settings rows all read the same volume for a harness, so a harness that is logged in shows as logged in everywhere, and one that isn't never shows as logged in anywhere.
The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every run. The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) shows whether each harness is logged in in its container, and can log it in again.

#### Guards
#### Volumes

The only volumes are one per harness, for its login and settings, ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness keeps it, owned and named by the application and shared by every project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them. Losing one costs only a login.
The harness's sessions are never kept in a volume. They are kept in the project, in `.suspense/sessions/`, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, one folder per conversation: `spec` for the spec lane's, and `questions` for the Ask tab's questions. Each run mounts only its own conversation's folder, read and write, where the harness keeps its sessions under its home, as Claude Code's ~/.claude/projects, never `.suspense/sessions/` as a whole, so no run sees another conversation's sessions. The application creates the folder before the run if it isn't there. So a conversation carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of the project, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.
Losing the project's sessions folder costs only the conversations'

content.text:
Your hunch was likely right: whether a harness was logged in was judged by running its own status command inside the container, and those checks don't agree with each other or with the login. Now login is checked, asked for, and run for the exact harness the run needs, and each harness's login is read the same way everywhere. The build is clean and the tests pass (one unrelated UI test timed out and passed on rerun), but I couldn't try a real Podman login here, so this is untested end to end.

- **Checking login:** "logged in" now means that harness's own credentials file is in its container volume and isn't empty: `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, `~/.codex/auth.json` or `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`. The login view, the Welcome check and Settings all use this one check, so they always agree.
- **Right harness:** a run that stops for lack of login now says which harness, such as "Codex isn't logged in", and its "Log in" button opens that harness's login rather than whatever the project on screen uses.
- **Failed logins:** the error now names the harness and the login command, gives its exit status, and quotes the last lines the command printed. If the command succeeds but writes no credentials, it says that instead.

Where the code differs from the spec:
- **Claude Code login command:** the spec says `claude /login`, but I kept `claude auth login`. Your installed Claude Code (2.1.281) has that command, while `claude /login` would start the full interactive session.
- **Codex login command:** it's `codex login --device-auth`, a device-code login, which the spec allows where offered. Codex and OpenCode aren't installed here, so I couldn't check their commands or credentials file paths.

If the project still asks for Claude Code, check its harness in Settings › Agent. A project with no saved harness uses the first agent in its `piton.config.pi`, which may be Claude Code.
